input_signals.name: SerialRepurchaser_Cheapness_Persistence
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), 0), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: Repeated, multi-year net repurchase is a credible (costly, hard-to-fake) signal of managerial conviction, so cheapness accompanied by a long history of net share retirement identifies persistent undervaluation, whereas cheap firms that have never retired shares are more likely value traps.
input_signals.reasoning: A single-year buyback can be opportunistic or cash-driven noise, so the count of net-repurchase years over five years measures the persistence of the financing state and scales the value signal by managerial credibility. Firms that are expensive get a near-zero valuation rank so their repurchase history contributes little, concentrating the signal in the cheap-and-committed corner.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ts_sum( indicator( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ), 0 ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: Value_Payout_ANDgate
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dvc, SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0))), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Mispricing requires joint confirmation: only firms that are simultaneously cheap on a revenue-based price multiple AND are net distributors of cash are reliably undervalued, and only firms that are simultaneously expensive AND net absorbers of equity are reliably overvalued; extremity on one theme alone should not place a firm in the tails.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the rank-sum with a rank product makes the construction a bilinear AND-gate — a firm cheap on sales-to-price but issuing equity is multiplied down toward the middle, which is exactly what the additive version failed to do. Sales-to-price is used instead of book-to-market so the valuation leg is not mechanically tied to the same accumulated-equity accounting that issuance itself inflates, and COALESCE keeps zero-flow firms in the sample.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sale, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( ratio( add( dvc, sub( coalesce( prstkc, 0 ), coalesce( sstk, 0 ) ) ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: EnterpriseCheapness_ConditionalCapitalFlow
input_signals.expression: SUB(MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(ADD(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), at)), 0)), MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che)))), INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), at), 0)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital-supply direction validates enterprise-level valuation: a cheap enterprise that is repaying total external capital (equity plus debt) is being discounted despite self-funding, whereas a richly valued enterprise absorbing external capital is exploiting favorable pricing of its whole capital structure; the valuation signal only "switches on" in the direction its capital flow corroborates.
input_signals.reasoning: The indicator gating means the enterprise multiple contributes only where financing agrees, so the test cannot be replicated by an additive average of the enterprise-multiple and external-financing anomalies, and off-diagonal firms receive attenuated (mid-range) rather than extreme scores. Debt financing is measured from the balance-sheet change in dltt+dlc instead of the sparsely populated dltis/dltr flow items, which preserves coverage while keeping the total-capital-flow economics intact.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( mul( rank( ratio( ebitda, sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ) ) ), indicator( neg( ratio( add( sub( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), delta( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ) ), at ) ), 0 ) ), mul( rank( neg( ratio( ebitda, sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ) ) ) ), indicator( ratio( add( sub( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), delta( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ) ), at ), 0 ) ) )

input_signals.name: IndustryCheap_NetCapitalReturn_Gate
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(SUB(RATIO(dvt, at), DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Undervaluation is confirmed only when a cheaply priced firm is a net returner of capital to all claimholders — distributing dividends while shrinking its liability base — whereas a richly priced firm that funds itself by expanding liabilities is being propped up by external capital; the two conditions must hold jointly to signal mispricing.
input_signals.reasoning: Both legs now use one construct per theme — an industry-relative EBITDA-to-price rank and a single net-capital-returned measure (total dividends less the change in the liability ratio) — so there is no long/short asymmetry mixing dividend yield against price-to-book. The multiplicative AND-gate is non-additive (unlike mirrored MIN or complementary-indicator forms, which collapse algebraically to a rank sum), and industry-relative valuation plus liability-flow financing keeps HML/CMA loading low while lt, dvt and at give far broader coverage than cash-flow-statement issuance items.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ebitda, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( sub( ratio( dvt, at ), delta( ratio( lt, at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ExternallyFundedPayout_at_HighMultiple
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), WINSOR(SUB(ADD(RATIO(dvt, at), RATIO(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), at)), RATIO(oancf, at)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Distributions that exceed internally generated cash must be funded by outside capital; a highly valued firm sustaining dividends and buybacks it cannot cover from operations is maintaining the appearance of shareholder returns with investors' own money, which marks overvaluation.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing MIN of two non-negative flows with the signed gap between total distributions and operating cash flow removes the tied mass at zero and gives a continuous, economically interpretable measure of payout that must be externally financed, so both tails are real portfolios. Because the excess-payout term is scaled by assets and the conditioning term is the price-to-book rank, the signal targets the overvaluation half of the story with a funding-sustainability mechanism no single-theme payout or issuance variable captures.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( mul( prcc_f, csho ), ceq ) ), winsor( sub( add( ratio( dvt, at ), ratio( coalesce( prstkc, 0 ), at ) ), ratio( oancf, at ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: GlamourGated_PayoutCoverageShortfall
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(SUB(ADD(RATIO(dvt, at), RATIO(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), at)), RATIO(oancf, at)), 1), INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 0.5))
input_signals.hypothesis: The payout-sustainability signal is informative only where the price embeds optimistic expectations: within the expensive half of the market, firms distributing beyond internal cash generation underperform firms retaining a large internal surplus, while among cheap firms the same gap mostly reflects cyclical earnings.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the continuous price-to-book weight with a hard median gate forces both tails strictly inside the glamour half, making the spread fully value-neutral instead of only approximately so, and cleanly separating "interaction" from "valuation-weighted main effect". Cheap firms are parked at exactly zero in the middle of the sort, so if this version retains the winner's alpha the interaction claim is validated, and if it loses it, the archived result was partly a valuation main effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( sub( add( ratio( dvt, at ), ratio( coalesce( prstkc, 0 ), at ) ), ratio( oancf, at ) ), 1 ), indicator( rank( ratio( mul( prcc_f, csho ), ceq ) ), 0.5 ) )

input_signals.name: EnterpriseRichness_PayoutShortfall
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che), sale)), WINSOR(SUB(ADD(RATIO(dvt, at), RATIO(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), at)), RATIO(oancf, at)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that fund distributions externally simultaneously become more levered, so an equity-only multiple mismeasures how richly the *whole business* is priced; grading the payout shortfall by enterprise-value-to-sales identifies overvalued businesses whose apparent shareholder returns are debt-financed.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates the valuation-metric axis of the winning mechanism: because uncovered payout mechanically raises leverage, price-to-book and the shortfall are entangled, whereas EV/sales prices the enterprise and is not inflated by the buyback itself. Using sales in the denominator also avoids the negative-book-equity distortion the critic flagged elsewhere, so the conditioning variable is well-defined for exactly the distressed-glamour firms that matter most.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ), sale ) ), winsor( sub( add( ratio( dvt, at ), ratio( coalesce( prstkc, 0 ), at ) ), ratio( oancf, at ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: NormalCashFlow_PayoutShortfall_Glamour
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(dvt, COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Sustainability should be judged against normal, not current, cash generation: a highly valued firm distributing more than its three-year average operating cash flow is structurally over-distributing, whereas one exceeding a single depressed year may simply be smoothing through a cyclical trough.
input_signals.reasoning: The temporal smoothing is required by the mechanism rather than decorative — the economic claim is about chronic dependence on outside funding, which a one-year cash-flow comparison conflates with transitory dips — so this variant should raise the signal-to-noise of the same interaction and improve FMB precision. It also predicts a lower turnover, more stable long-short composition than the one-year version, which speaks to the objective's stability diagnostic.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( mul( prcc_f, csho ), ceq ) ), winsor( sub( ratio( add( dvt, coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ), ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: CashReserveDepletion_Distribution_Glamour
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), MUL(RATIO(ADD(dvt, COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A richly valued firm that distributes cash while its liquidity reserves are shrinking is liquidating balance-sheet slack to sustain payouts, which is the least sustainable funding source of all; the same distribution alongside a growing cash pile signals genuine surplus generation.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the equity-issuance channel entirely — so it cannot be a reweighting of the net-issuance anomaly — and instead names the third possible funding source for distributions: internal liquidity depletion, complementing the creditor-funded version already accepted this round. Together the two accepted funding-source signals and this one decompose *how* rich firms pay for distributions they cannot earn, which is a sharper economic question than the issuance-size interaction I proposed.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( mul( prcc_f, csho ), ceq ) ), mul( ratio( add( dvt, coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ), neg( winsor( delta( ratio( che, at ), 1 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ActiveFinancing_CashFlowYieldCheapness
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), WINSOR(ABS(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: The mispricing that own-equity transactions reveal is best measured against realized cash generation rather than sales, since cash flow is the quantity managers actually compare with the market price when deciding whether to buy or sell shares.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates the valuation-metric axis of the same mechanism, replacing an industry-relative sales multiple with an industry-relative operating-cash-flow yield, and it matters economically because gen-4 evidence showed the cash-flow dimension carries independent return information among expensive firms. The cost is coverage (~0.09 because oancf starts later), so comparing it with Signal 1 tells us whether the metric or the sample is driving the result.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ind_zscore( ratio( oancf, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 1 ), winsor( abs( ratio( sub( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: CashYieldCheapness_x_SmoothedActivity
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), MA(WINSOR(ABS(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at)), 1), 3))
input_signals.hypothesis: Active management of the share base is a persistent policy rather than a one-year event, so the average transaction intensity over three years should identify participating firms more reliably than a single year's flow, which is contaminated by lumpy one-off deals.
input_signals.reasoning: This tests whether the amplifier is a *state* or an *event*, using magnitudes and the cash-flow-yield anchor — the two ingredients the earlier count-based chronic-engagement attempt lacked when it failed with a sales multiple. Smoothing should also cut turnover in the sorted portfolio, so a comparable alpha with a higher t-statistic would be the ideal outcome for the objective.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ind_zscore( ratio( oancf, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 1 ), ma( winsor( abs( ratio( sub( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ) ), 1 ), 3 ) )

input_signals.name: CashYieldCheapness_x_CreditorActivity
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), WINSOR(ABS(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: If the mechanism is that cheapness gets validated when informed capital providers transact with the firm, then activity in the credit market should amplify the valuation signal just as equity activity does; if instead the mechanism is specific to management trading its own mispriced shares, only equity activity should work.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the decisive channel test for the winning family — same valuation anchor, same direction-free absolute-intensity construction, but the transaction counterparty is creditors rather than shareholders — and it carries no equity-flow information at all, so the two results cannot be mechanically related. A null here combined with a strong equity result would establish that the interaction is specifically about the firm trading its *own equity* against its own valuation.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ind_zscore( ratio( oancf, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 1 ), winsor( abs( delta( ratio( lt, at ), 1 ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: CashYieldCheapness_x_GrossShareTurnover
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: The relevant amplifier is the gross volume a firm transacts in its own shares, not the net change in equity supply: a firm issuing five percent and retiring five percent in the same year has zero net flow yet is intensely engaged in pricing its own equity, and its valuation signal should be just as informative.
input_signals.reasoning: Gross turnover and absolute net flow diverge exactly for firms running simultaneous issuance and repurchase programs, so this cleanly separates "transaction volume" from "net supply change" — and unlike an earlier MIN-based attempt at simultaneity it is continuous with no tied mass, since almost all firms have some gross flow. If gross turnover works at least as well as absolute net flow, the mechanism is participation in one's own market rather than the net-issuance anomaly wearing a new scaling.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ind_zscore( ratio( oancf, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 1 ), winsor( ratio( add( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: EnterpriseCashYieldCheapness_x_EquityActivity
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), 1), WINSOR(ABS(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that transact heavily in their own equity change their leverage in the process, which distorts an equity-only cheapness measure; pricing the whole enterprise against its operating profits gives a cheapness anchor that is invariant to the financing transaction being used as the amplifier.
input_signals.reasoning: This removes a genuine mechanical contamination in the winning design — a large buyback shrinks equity value and mechanically raises an equity-based cash yield, while a large issue does the reverse — so an enterprise-level anchor tests whether the archived alpha reflects mispricing or that accounting artifact. Coverage stays at the full ~0.13 because it uses EBITDA and balance-sheet debt rather than oancf.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ind_zscore( ratio( ebitda, sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ) ) ), 1 ), winsor( abs( ratio( sub( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: HighlyActiveFirms_CashYieldCheapness
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), INDICATOR(IND_RANK(ABS(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at))), 0.7))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheapness relative to industry peers on cash generation predicts returns only among firms that are unusually active transactors of their own equity by their industry's own standards; for firms transacting at or below their industry norm the same valuation gap carries no information because nobody inside the firm is acting on it.
input_signals.reasoning: Unlike the rank-weighted version, this does not flatten the interaction — inactive firms receive exactly zero rather than a half-weight, so they sit in the middle of the sort and both tails consist solely of the most active transactors, which is what the mechanism claims. Judging activity by within-industry percentile rather than raw dollars-over-assets also removes the persistent cross-industry composition (routine issuers such as development-stage biotech versus utilities) that drives the raw amplifier's tails into small, volatile firms, and dropping magnitude weighting entirely tests whether flow size is needed at all or merely participation.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ind_zscore( ratio( oancf, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 1 ), indicator( ind_rank( abs( ratio( sub( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ) ) ), 0.7 ) )

input_signals.name: EnterpriseYield_x_GrossTurnover_FullPanel
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: The same mechanism should operate over the whole panel if cheapness is anchored at the enterprise level, since enterprise value is not mechanically distorted by the very equity transactions used as the amplifier and EBITDA is reported decades earlier than operating cash flow.
input_signals.reasoning: The full-coverage EBITDA-to-market anchor failed (fmb 0.058) while the enterprise anchor partially survived (fmb 2.02, alpha +2.0%) with the weaker net-flow amplifier, so this pairing — best full-coverage anchor with best amplifier — is the natural and untested combination and is the only route to a strong result at 0.14 coverage rather than 0.09. A strong outcome here would also settle whether the archive's leading results are a post-1988 subsample artifact.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ind_zscore( ratio( ebitda, sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ) ) ), 1 ), winsor( ratio( add( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: CashYield_x_RepurchaseLeg
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), at), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: If the theme's original economic story is correct, the amplification should come specifically from the buyback leg: cheap firms retiring shares are the corner where management confirms undervaluation, and gross repurchase intensity alone should carry the interaction.
input_signals.reasoning: This decomposes the winning gross-turnover amplifier into its repurchase component so we can attribute the +4.2% alpha, which no archive entry has done; paired with Signal 6 it distinguishes the classic managerial-confirmation story from a symmetric participation effect. Interpretation matters now because only two generations remain and the final consolidation should be built on the component that actually carries the alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ind_zscore( ratio( oancf, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 1 ), winsor( ratio( coalesce( prstkc, 0 ), at ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: CashYield_x_IssuanceLeg
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(sstk, 0), at), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: The mirror decomposition: if the mechanism is participation rather than managerial confirmation, then cheapness should also be amplified among heavy issuers, because a firm selling stock while priced cheaply against its own cash generation is the sharpest case of a valuation gap being transacted against.
input_signals.reasoning: Together with Signal 5 this is a clean two-way attribution of the archive's best amplifier at identical anchor, coverage and scaling, so any difference in alpha is interpretable as directional content rather than construction. A strong result on both legs would establish the participation mechanism as genuinely two-sided, which is the most novel claim this research line has produced.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ind_zscore( ratio( oancf, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 1 ), winsor( ratio( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), at ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: NormalizedCashYield_x_GrossTurnover
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(MA(oancf, 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year of operating cash flow is a noisy estimate of the cash-generating power a manager compares with the market price; cheapness measured against three-year average cash generation identifies genuinely mispriced firms, and that cleaner anchor should transmit more strongly through the transaction-intensity amplifier.
input_signals.reasoning: Every refinement tested so far has been on the amplifier side, yet the archive's evidence is that the *anchor* is the binding constraint — holding the amplifier fixed, FMB t-statistics ranged from 0.06 to 3.7 purely on the choice of valuation metric — so smoothing the fundamental in the numerator attacks the component that actually determines power. This is a different economic claim from smoothing the amplifier (transitory cash-flow measurement error versus lumpy transaction timing) and leaves the transaction measure at its best-performing one-year gross form.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ind_zscore( ratio( ma( oancf, 3 ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 1 ), winsor( ratio( add( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: CashYield_x_EngagementSurprise
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), MA(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 3)), 1), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), MA(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 3)), 0)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Routine share turnover — annual option exercise, standing repurchase authorisations — reveals nothing, whereas a surge in own-equity transaction volume above the firm's own recent norm marks the moment management chooses to act on a valuation gap; only that surprise component should amplify cheapness.
input_signals.reasoning: This poses the event-versus-state question that the accepted smoothed-amplifier signal cannot answer: smoothing asserts participation is a persistent policy, whereas this asserts it is the deviation from policy that carries information, and the two make opposite predictions about which construction should dominate. The deviation is truncated at zero so the amplifier stays non-negative and firms transacting at or below their norm sit in the middle of the sort rather than flipping the sign of the cheapness anchor.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ind_zscore( ratio( oancf, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 1 ), mul( winsor( sub( ratio( add( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ), ma( ratio( add( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ), 3 ) ), 1 ), indicator( sub( ratio( add( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ), ma( ratio( add( coalesce( sstk, 0 ), coalesce( prstkc, 0 ) ), at ), 3 ) ), 0 ) ) )

input_signals.name: CashYield_x_PeerExcessTurnover
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), MUL(WINSOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at)), 1), INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at)), 0)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What counts as active participation in one's own equity is industry-specific — development-stage biotechs issue as a matter of course while utilities almost never do — so the informative amplifier is transaction volume in excess of the industry norm, not the raw level, which mostly encodes industry identity and firm size.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the raw amplifier with its industry-demeaned, one-sided excess directly addresses the standing objection that the archive's tails are concentrated in small, chronically high-issuance firms, since it removes the persistent cross-industry composition that drives that concentration while keeping continuous magnitude information the earlier 70th-percentile indicator discarded. If alpha holds with a peer-relative amplifier, the mechanism is genuine deviation-from-norm participation rather than a sector and size tilt.
input_signals.author: proposer
